Family Health

Penile swelling: causes, warning signs and treatment

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Swelling of the penis may be uncomfortable, worrying or embarrassing to discuss. The cause can range from a contact reaction to a condition that needs urgent treatment, so the associated symptoms and timing matter.

Start with the symptoms that cannot wait

A swollen penis can result from irritation, inflammation, infection, injury or a problem affecting blood flow. Pain, itching, a change in colour, discharge and difficulty urinating provide useful clues, but they cannot reliably identify the cause at home. The first decision is whether urgent assessment is needed.

Go to emergency care for a foreskin trapped behind the head of the penis, inability to pass urine, rapidly worsening severe pain or swelling, or a serious injury. A persistent erection approaching three to four hours is also an emergency; with sickle cell disease, a painful erection lasting more than one hour needs emergency help. Do not wait for every symptom on a checklist to appear.

Notice where the swelling is and what changed

The head of the penis is called the glans, the skin covering it is the foreskin, and the urine outlet connects to the urethra. Swelling may involve one of these areas or the shaft. A clinician will also ask whether it began suddenly, followed sex or injury, appeared after a new product, or has happened before.

Describe redness or another colour change, tenderness, burning, itching, sores, bumps, an unusual smell and any discharge. On darker skin, redness may be less obvious, so discomfort and a change from the usual appearance still matter. Mention painful urination, a change in the urinary stream and pain during sex or erections.

Balanitis: inflammation of the head of the penis

Balanitis can make the glans sore, swollen and itchy. The skin may look red or shiny, and there may be small sore areas, an unpleasant smell or material under the foreskin. Passing urine may sting. Sometimes the foreskin becomes harder to move because the surrounding tissue is inflamed.

Yeast, including Candida, is one possible cause, but bacteria, irritation and skin conditions can produce similar symptoms. It is not appropriate to assume every episode is fungal or to rank one organism as the cause without an assessment. Recurrent or severe episodes may lead to checks for diabetes or another condition affecting infection risk.

Having balanitis does not by itself establish a sexually transmitted infection or indicate poor personal care. Some infections can pass between partners, so testing and partner advice depend on the actual cause. Repeated harsh washing can also worsen irritation rather than solve it.

Contact reactions to condoms, lubricants and skin products

A contact reaction occurs when a substance irritates the skin or triggers an allergy. Possible exposures include latex, ingredients such as propylene glycol in some lubricants, spermicides, fragranced soaps and lotions, or pool chemicals. A reaction may involve dryness, itching, burning, redness, little bumps or blisters as well as swelling.

Stop using a newly introduced product while you arrange advice, and keep its packaging or ingredient list. This can help distinguish a likely exposure from an unrelated infection. Do not repeatedly test a suspected allergy on inflamed genital skin or replace one scented product with another.

If condoms may be involved, ask about a suitable non-latex option and lubricant compatibility. Avoiding a trigger should not mean abandoning STI or pregnancy protection without an alternative. Swelling together with breathing difficulty or widespread allergic symptoms needs emergency help.

Urethritis: inflammation of the urine channel

Urethritis can cause burning when urinating, irritation at the opening and white, yellow or other unusual discharge. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia are important infectious causes, while nongonococcal urethritis describes inflammation not attributed to gonorrhoea rather than one particular organism. Chemical irritation or instrumentation, such as a catheter, can also be relevant.

Urethritis is not simply another name for a bladder infection. The location, exposure history and tests guide treatment. A urine sample or swab may be used to look for infection; a clinician may recommend additional sexual-health tests. Avoid leftover antibiotics, which may not treat the cause and can complicate later assessment.

Posthitis: when the foreskin is inflamed

Posthitis refers to inflammation of the foreskin itself. It may be tender, red or swollen, and moving it can become uncomfortable. A tight feeling or material underneath the skin may accompany the symptoms. Yeast is a possible contributor, but the name does not prove a yeast infection.

Friction, irritants and other infections or skin disorders can affect this area. Smegma is a mixture of skin cells and oils that can collect beneath a retractable foreskin; its presence alone is not a diagnosis. Painful or recurrent inflammation deserves review rather than increasingly forceful cleaning.

Balanoposthitis: inflammation in both areas

When the glans and foreskin are both inflamed, clinicians may use the term balanoposthitis. Swelling, pain, itching and an unpleasant discharge or smell can occur together. The foreskin may be difficult to move, particularly when the tissues are already sore.

This term describes which tissues are affected, not a separate organism that every patient has. Treatment depends on the cause and on whether urine can pass normally. Persistent episodes may require a review of skin care, infection testing, diabetes risk or the foreskin itself. Do not treat a published percentage as a prediction of your own diagnosis.

Paraphimosis: a foreskin trapped behind the glans

Paraphimosis happens when a retracted foreskin cannot be brought forward to cover the head of the penis. A tight band can trap swelling and impair blood flow. Pain, tenderness and increasing swelling may follow, and the glans can change colour. This requires emergency assessment even if urine is still passing.

It can happen after cleaning, sex or a medical procedure if the foreskin remains pulled back. Inflammation or injury may contribute. Do not keep squeezing, stretching or trying home reduction methods while waiting to see whether it resolves. Prompt treatment is important to protect the tissue.

Phimosis is different: the foreskin is too tight to retract in the first place. A non-retractable foreskin can be normal in a young child and should not be forced back. In anyone whose foreskin retracts comfortably, returning it to its usual forward position after washing helps avoid it becoming trapped.

Priapism: an erection that does not settle

Priapism is an erection that persists beyond sexual stimulation or occurs without it. In the ischaemic form, blood is trapped and the shaft may be rigid and painful while the glans is softer. A different, non-ischaemic form may follow injury and be less rigid or less painful. These patterns are not reliable self-diagnostic tests.

Blood disorders such as sickle cell disease, some medicines and erectile-dysfunction treatments, and recreational drugs can be relevant. Tell the emergency team about injections, tablets and any recent injury, including injury to the perineum between the genitals and anus. Do not be embarrassed to give an accurate account.

Get emergency care for the durations described above, and seek advice earlier if pain is severe or the erection is not resolving. Ice or cold water is not a safe general remedy for priapism, particularly with sickle cell disease. Sex or masturbation should not be used to delay care. Hospital treatment may involve medication, drainage or a procedure according to the type.

Peyronie’s disease: a scar plaque and changing shape

Peyronie’s disease involves scar tissue in the covering around the erectile tissue. It can cause a firm area, curvature, shortening, painful erections or difficulty with intercourse. During an evolving phase there may be pain and change; later the condition can become more stable. Not every naturally curved penis has this disorder.

An injury during sex or another activity may contribute, sometimes without a memorable single event. Connective-tissue conditions, age and other individual factors can also matter. It is not caused by dirt under the foreskin and is not a contagious infection. Younger adults can be affected, although risk changes with age.

Arrange a urology review for a new curve, a palpable plaque or erections that become painful or less functional. Evaluation and treatment depend on the stage and impact. Do not try to straighten a painful erection by force or infer the diagnosis from a general prevalence statistic.

Injury can require its own urgent pathway

Swelling after an injury should not automatically be treated as a skin infection. A sudden pop or crack during an erection, immediate loss of the erection, marked pain and rapid bruising can indicate a penile fracture. Despite the name, this involves a tear in the erectile-tissue covering rather than a broken bone.

Blood at the urine opening, visible blood in urine or difficulty passing urine after trauma can indicate an associated urinary injury. Seek urgent care rather than testing whether sex is still possible or waiting for a bruise to fade. Tell the clinician when and how it happened so the appropriate examination and tests can be selected.

Persistent skin changes need assessment, including for cancer

Penile cancer is uncommon, and many lumps or sore areas have other causes. Nevertheless, a growth, thickened area, persistent sore, bleeding, unexplained discharge or a changing patch of skin should be examined. A blue, brown, red or other colour change is not enough on its own to distinguish a harmless lesion from something that needs investigation.

Risk is associated with factors including increasing age, certain HPV infections, smoking and some foreskin or immune-system problems. These factors do not mean a person will develop cancer, and their absence does not make a persistent lesion safe to ignore. The condition should not be framed as punishment for poor hygiene.

Arrange an appointment promptly rather than repeatedly applying creams to a lesion that does not heal. A clinician may refer you for specialist assessment or a biopsy. Early assessment also helps identify non-cancerous skin conditions that need a different treatment from an infection.

What a clinician may ask and examine

Expect questions about the timing, discomfort, urination, erections, sexual contact, recent injury and products used on the skin. Medicines, diabetes, immune conditions and previous similar episodes are relevant. An accurate account helps care; it is not an invitation to judge someone’s sex life or hygiene.

The examination may identify the affected tissues, the position of the foreskin, a rash, discharge, plaque or injury. You can ask for an explanation before each step and request a chaperone. A physical examination is often central, but it does not always establish the cause without testing or follow-up.

Swabs, urine tests and scans answer different questions

A swab can help investigate discharge or a suspected infection. Urine testing may assess urinary symptoms or look for sexually transmitted organisms, depending on the sample and test requested. Blood tests, including a diabetes check in selected cases, are sometimes useful when inflammation is severe or repeatedly returns.

Ultrasound and other imaging are selected for a particular concern, such as blood flow, a deeper injury or an uncertain structural problem. X-rays, CT and MRI are not interchangeable routine tests for every swollen penis. A persistent suspicious skin lesion may require a tissue sample rather than a scan alone.

Treatment should follow the cause

An antifungal may be used for a fungal infection, an antibiotic for a bacterial cause, or a prescribed anti-inflammatory cream for an appropriate skin condition. Some situations need an oral medicine; severe infection may need hospital care and intravenous treatment. A cream that helped someone else may be wrong for your symptoms.

Paraphimosis and priapism require their own urgent treatment. In selected foreskin problems, a clinician may recommend a dorsal slit, an incision that releases the tight skin, or circumcision. These are not routine treatments for all swelling. Ask why a procedure is recommended, what alternatives exist and how recovery will be managed.

Pain relief can be part of care, but it does not correct impaired circulation, a trapped foreskin or an injury. Ask which medicine is suitable for your health conditions and other treatment. Do not use temporary improvement in pain as proof that an emergency has resolved.

Gentle care while you arrange advice

For mild surface irritation without urgent warning signs, wash gently with lukewarm water and pat dry. Avoid fragranced soaps, deodorants, harsh antiseptics and vigorous scrubbing. If the foreskin moves comfortably, handle it gently and return it to its usual position; never force a tight or painful foreskin.

A warm rinse may ease discomfort, but bathing is not treatment for a trapped foreskin, persistent erection or significant infection. Ice packs and pressure are not universal treatments for undiagnosed swelling. Follow condition-specific advice, and do not keep trying home measures while pain, colour change or urinary difficulty worsens.

Sex, partners and prevention of recurrence

Avoid activity that rubs or hurts inflamed tissue. If urethritis or an STI is suspected, ask the treating service when sex can safely resume and whether partners need testing or treatment. Treating only one person may leave a route for reinfection; a skin irritation, however, does not automatically mean both partners need antibiotics.

Once the cause is clearer, prevention can be specific: replacing an irritant, improving comfortable skin care, treating a recurrent infection or addressing a foreskin problem. Keep the diagnosis and product names so future episodes are not automatically treated as the same condition without reassessment.

Know when the follow-up plan needs to change

Return for review if swelling persists, recurs or becomes worse despite treatment. New sores, discharge, painful erections or an altered urinary stream are reasons to contact the clinician. Ask how soon improvement should occur and what to do if the first treatment does not help.

Seek emergency help for a trapped retracted foreskin, a prolonged erection, inability to urinate, a serious injury or rapidly worsening severe symptoms. A person can need urgent care without knowing the medical name of the problem. The goal is timely assessment and treatment that matches the cause, not a diagnosis made from appearance alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Separate a skin or infection problem from a trapped foreskin, prolonged erection or significant injury before trying home treatment.

Tests and medicines depend on the cause. Persistent lesions, recurrent inflammation and changes in urination or erections need follow-up.

How BeMama can help

Bring the names of medicines and skin products, and explain the timing honestly. A clear history helps a clinician choose the right assessment.

When to seek help

Emergency warning signs should lead to immediate local medical care, not a trial of creams, pressure or ice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Balanitis, posthitis and balanoposthitis describe inflamed areas rather than one proven infection.
  • Paraphimosis and prolonged erections can threaten tissue and need urgent care.
  • A new curve, injury or persistent skin lesion needs its own assessment.
  • Gentle care and a cause-specific follow-up plan are safer than repeated unsupervised treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Does swelling always mean an STI?

No. Irritation, skin disease, injury and several non-infectious conditions can cause swelling. Sexual-health testing may still be appropriate when the symptoms or exposure history suggest it.

What is the difference between balanitis and balanoposthitis?

Balanitis affects the glans; posthitis affects the foreskin. Balanoposthitis describes inflammation in both. These names do not establish whether yeast, bacteria or an irritant is responsible.

Is a trapped foreskin urgent if I can still urinate?

Yes. A foreskin stuck behind the glans is paraphimosis and needs emergency assessment because circulation can be affected even before urine stops passing.

When does a persistent erection need emergency care?

An erection lasting more than three to four hours needs emergency care. With sickle cell disease, a painful erection lasting more than one hour needs emergency help. Seek advice earlier for severe pain or concern; do not wait to try ice or sex.

Can I use an ice pack for every type of swelling?

No. Treatment depends on the cause. Ice or cold water can worsen priapism, particularly with sickle cell disease, and should not delay emergency assessment.

Should I force my child’s foreskin back to clean it?

No. Non-retractability can be normal in children. Forced retraction can injure the tissue. Seek advice for pain, inflammation or urinary difficulty.

Does a new curve mean Peyronie’s disease?

Not necessarily, but a new curve, firm plaque or painful erection deserves assessment. Peyronie’s involves scar tissue and is different from ordinary surface irritation or a naturally curved penis.

Will everyone need a scan?

No. Examination, a swab or urine testing may be more useful initially. Imaging or biopsy is chosen for a specific concern rather than ordered as a standard package.

Can I use leftover antifungal or antibiotic treatment?

Avoid choosing treatment solely because the symptoms look familiar. Different causes can appear similar, and persistent or recurrent swelling should be reassessed.

Does a persistent sore mean cancer?

Many sores have other causes, but a lesion that persists, bleeds or changes needs examination. Do not keep applying creams without a diagnosis or assume an absent risk factor rules cancer out.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
